result.topic: PAN-OS/Panorama XML+REST API keygen flow: request/response shape, key interchangeability, default lifetime, and concurrent-generation safety

confirmedFacts.claim: type=keygen request shape is POST https://<host>/api/?type=keygen with form-encoded user=<user>&password=<password> (GET with the same params also works for the XML API). Same mechanism against a firewall's own hostname or Panorama's own hostname -- no separate REST-specific keygen endpoint exists.

keygen request params match project code exactly: pan-python's reference implementation builds query={'type':'keygen','user':...,'password':...} and POSTs (or GETs if use_get set) form/query-encoded, identical to pan_auth.py's requests.post(data={'type':'keygen','user':...,'password':...}).
confirmedFacts.evidence: query = {'type': 'keygen', 'user': self.api_username, 'password': self.api_password}; data = urlencode(query); request = Request(url, data.encode())  # POST unless self.use_get

confirmedFacts.claim: The successful keygen response envelope is <response status="success"><result><key>...</key></result></response> -- i.e. the key IS literally at ./result/key relative to the <response> root, exactly as pan_auth.py's root.findtext('./result/key') assumes. This closes the project's previously-flagged 'unconfirmed response shape' gap.

Independent corroboration of the ./result/key path from the reference open-source SDK's actual parsing code (not just docs prose): keygen() does root.find('result') then .find('key'), raising an error if absent.
confirmedFacts.evidence: self.element_result = self.element_root.find('result'); element = self.element_result.find('key'); if element is None: raise PanXapiError('keygen(): key element not found'); self.api_key = element.text

confirmedFacts.claim: By default, PAN-OS API Key Lifetime = 0, meaning keys never expire on their own. An admin must explicitly configure a lifetime (1-525600 minutes) or click 'Expire all API Keys' under Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings for keys to stop working over time.
confirmedFacts.evidence: By default, the API key lifetime is set to 0, which means that the keys will never expire. ... you must specify a validity period that ranges between 1-525600 minutes.

confirmedFacts.claim: The API key is derived from (encrypted with) the admin's username+password plus, since PAN-OS 9.0, an embedded generation timestamp -- it is not a server-stored 'current active key' slot. Generating an additional key for the same admin does NOT invalidate previously generated keys; multiple keys remain simultaneously valid. Keys are invalidated only by: (a) changing that admin's password, (b) explicitly clicking 'Expire/Revoke all API Keys' (which stamps a cutoff timestamp), (c) the configured Lifetime elapsing, or (d) turning on certificate-based API key encryption.
confirmedFacts.evidence: PAN-OS >= 9.0 adds a timestamp to the API keys (encrypted with the username and password) ... 'Revoke all keys' ... adds a timestamp to the configuration that makes all keys using an inferior timestamp unusable. To revoke a key for a given user, the only way is to change that user's password.

confirmedFacts.claim: Corroborating the above from a second, independent line: PAN-OS 9.0+ allows creating multiple keys per admin and none are invalidated just by generating another.
confirmedFacts.evidence: In PAN-OS 9.0 and later, you are able to create multiple keys and they are all valid ... none of the previously generated API keys are being invalidated

confirmedFacts.claim: Given the above (keys are independently valid, no server-side single-slot state to race on), the reference SDK does NOT implement any client-side locking/mutex around keygen or its lazy api_key caching -- it relies purely on the device-side non-mutual-invalidation behavior rather than serializing calls.
confirmedFacts.evidence: if self.api_key is None: self.keygen() -- classic check-then-act with no lock; no threading/locking primitives imported or used anywhere in the module.

confirmedFacts.claim: Palo Alto's own best-practice guidance is to limit total concurrent API calls (of any type, keygen included) against one device to 5, purely for management-plane web-server performance reasons -- this is a soft best practice, not a documented hard-enforced or keygen-specific limit.
confirmedFacts.evidence: Limit the number of concurrent API calls to five ... to ensure there is no performance impact to the firewall web interface, as the management plane web server handles requests from both the API and the web interface.

confirmedFacts.claim: REST API key delivery is X-PAN-KEY header only (matches project assumption); XML API accepts either the X-PAN-KEY header or a key=<apikey> query parameter. Both surfaces document the identical header name/mechanism, and REST's own 'get your key' instruction is simply 'use your administrative credentials to get an API key' with no separate procedure described -- structurally consistent with one shared key, but no single official sentence explicitly states 'the same key value works on both APIs.'
confirmedFacts.evidence: You can enter the key with the custom HTTP header X-PAN-KEY: <key>

remainingGaps: No single official docs.paloaltonetworks.com or pan.dev sentence explicitly states 'a key generated via type=keygen is valid for both XML API and REST API calls interchangeably' -- the conclusion is structural/circumstantial (one shared keygen endpoint, identical X-PAN-KEY mechanism referenced on both API surfaces' auth pages, Admin Role Profiles treat XML API tab and REST API tab as two permission toggles on the SAME account rather than two credential systems). Needs a live-device test: generate one key via type=keygen, use it in an X-PAN-KEY REST call and separately in an XML API call.

The exact keygen response XML (status/result/key) was only recoverable via search-engine snippet extraction of the live docs.paloaltonetworks.com page's rendered content -- direct WebFetch of that same URL repeatedly failed to surface the block verbatim (likely JS-rendered content the fetch tool's HTML-to-markdown pass didn't capture). The pan-python source-code confirmation of ./result/key is solid and independent, but if 100% certainty on the doc page itself is required, a manual browser visit to https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/ngfw/api/api-authentication-and-security/generate-api-key is worth doing.

A claim surfaced twice during search-engine synthesis ('if you generate another key for the same user, all existing sessions will end for the user and previous API sessions will be deleted') could NOT be traced to any locatable primary source despite an exact-phrase search, and it directly contradicts the better-sourced, cross-corroborated finding (PAN-OS 9.0 timestamp mechanism + KCS article) that multiple generated keys coexist validly. Treated as likely search-synthesis noise/hallucination, not used as a confirmed fact -- but flagging it because it bears directly on the concurrency-safety question and a live device is the only way to fully rule it out (generate 2 keys back-to-back for the same admin, confirm both still authenticate afterward).

No official page states whether PAN-OS enforces any rate limit specifically on type=keygen (as distinct from the general 'limit concurrent API calls to 5' best practice for all API call types combined).

Whether the 5-concurrent-calls best practice is enforced identically on Panorama vs. a standalone firewall, and whether it would actually reject (not just slow) a burst of near-simultaneous keygen calls from multiple threads for one admin, is not documented -- untested against a real device.

recommendedCodeChanges.change: Upgrade the module docstring block (currently lines ~23-32, the 'NOT CONFIRMED: the literal XML response body...' paragraph) from 'unconfirmed, pattern-guessed' to 'confirmed'. The ./result/key path is now backed by two independent sources: the official docs.paloaltonetworks.com generate-api-key page's quoted response body (<response status="success"><result><key>...</key></result></response>) and pan-python's lib/pan/xapi.py keygen() implementation, which parses the identical path (root.find('result').find('key')). Keep the existing runtime defensive check/log (cheap insurance) but drop the 'this exact path has not been verified' language and cite these two sources instead.

PanAuthClient.api_key()'s lazy-init ('if self._api_key is None: self._api_key = self._generate_key()') is a classic check-then-act race with no lock, matching pan-python's own reference implementation (which also has no lock). Research shows this is not a correctness bug today -- PAN-OS does not invalidate one generated key when another is generated for the same admin, so concurrent first-use calls would at worst produce a few redundant-but-independently-valid keys and duplicate network round-trips, not corruption or lockout. main.py is currently fully sequential so this is not live. If/when the collector is parallelized across devices or within a device's calls, add a threading.Lock around the check-and-generate in api_key() purely to avoid wasteful duplicate keygen round-trips -- not required for correctness per current findings, but cheap and removes the ambiguity.

In section 1 (Authentication), replace the 'Open gap' bullet about XML/REST key validation with the more complete, cited picture from this research: (a) key interchangeability across XML/REST remains formally unconfirmed by any single official sentence but is now backed by stronger structural evidence (cite generate-api-key page + rest-api-request-response-structure page + pan-os-api-authentication page); (b) add a new fact, with citations, that generating additional keys for the same admin does not invalidate earlier ones (only password change / Expire-all-Keys / Lifetime elapse / cert-encryption toggle do) -- this is directly relevant if the project ever considers per-device or cross-device parallel collection.
